docs.title: Terraform Resource Types Are Nouns, Not Commands 🏷️📦
docs.text:
A resource type is the most fundamental unit in a Terraform configuration, and it is also the most commonly misread:

resource "local_file" "my_server" {
  filename = "server_config.txt"
  content  = "Server is running perfectly."
}

local_file here means a file — the object itself, not an action performed on it. That distinction is the foundational premise of declarative infrastructure.

docs.title: 🏷️ The Block Header Declares the Noun
docs.text:
resource "local_file" "my_server" {
#  ▲           ▲              ▲
#  │           │              └─ 2. Resource Name
#  │           └──────────────── 1. Resource Type
#  └──────────────────────────── Block Keyword

Two labels follow the resource keyword:

  1. "local_file" (Resource Type): Defined by the provider implementing it. This represents the category or entity: "a file".
  2. "my_server" (Resource Name): Chosen by you. This is Terraform's internal handle for this specific instance of that category — used in the state file, in CLI output, and whenever referencing this resource elsewhere in code (local_file.my_server.id). It has no bearing on the actual filename on disk.

docs.title: 📋 What's Inside the Block: Attributes, Not Instructions
docs.text:
filename = "server_config.txt"
content  = "Server is running perfectly."

These are attributes — they describe what the noun should look like once it exists, not the procedural steps needed to create it.

It is conceptually identical to declaring a configuration object:

{
  "file": {
    "filename": "server_config.txt",
    "content": "Server is running perfectly."
  }
}

No verb appears anywhere in that data structure, and none appears in HCL either:

  • You specify the entity's properties (its path, its content), not an imperative command to write them.
  • Whether Terraform performs an actual disk write or API call is evaluated separately by diffing these declared attributes against the current state.
  • If nothing differs, nothing happens. The content line remains in your configuration on every run, but triggers zero side effects.

[!NOTE] This is why a declarative configuration block can be applied repeatedly without unintended side effects (idempotency). It never described an action to repeat; it described a target state, and that state either holds or it doesn't.

docs.title: ⚡ The Verbs Live Entirely in the CLI
docs.text:
Because resource types express no action, the lifecycle verbs (create, read, update, destroy) are handled outside the .tf files entirely. They are driven by the CLI commands executed against the whole configuration:

terraform plan     # Compute the diff between declared and actual state
terraform apply    # Execute whichever CRUD operations that diff requires
terraform destroy  # Remove all managed infrastructure in dependency order

You will never see a resource type paired with an imperative verb — there is no create_local_file or local_file.write(). The type remains a pure noun:

Imperative Thinking (Scripts) Declarative Reality (Terraform) create_vm(size="t3.micro") resource "aws_instance" "web" { instance_type = "t3.micro" } put_file(name="app.conf") resource "local_file" "app_conf" { filename = "app.conf" } update_bucket_policy(id) resource "aws_s3_bucket_policy" "main" { ... }

Terraform decides based on the delta whether create, update, or destroy applies on any given run — that operational decision never lives inside your .tf file.

docs.title: 🌐 Every Provider Defines Its Own Nouns
docs.text:
Terraform's core engine has zero built-in resource types. Every noun is owned by an external provider plugin, scoped to the objects exposed by that target platform:

Provider Prefix Example Nouns (Resource Types) Managed Entity AWS aws_ aws_instance, aws_s3_bucket, aws_vpc Cloud infrastructure Azure azurerm_ azurerm_virtual_machine, azurerm_resource_group Azure resources Google Cloud google_ google_compute_instance, google_storage_bucket GCP assets Kubernetes kubernetes_ kubernetes_deployment, kubernetes_namespace Cluster objects Local local_ local_file, local_sensitive_file Filesystem items

The standard naming convention — <provider>_<object> — remains consistent across the ecosystem. There is no static master list to memorize: the Terraform Registry for each provider serves as the authoritative source of truth, expanding as providers expose new platform capabilities.

docs.title: 🚀 Bulletproofing Your Terraform State with S3 Versioning
docs.text:
In Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform, your terraform.tfstate file is the absolute source of truth for your cloud environment. If you lose or corrupt this file, Terraform loses its memory — leading to duplicate resources, orphaned infrastructure, or catastrophic accidental deletions.

To protect against state loss, implementing S3 Bucket Versioning (aws_s3_bucket_versioning) is strictly mandatory for production environments.

docs.title: 🛑 Part 1: Why S3 Versioning Is Strictly Necessary
docs.text:
Before writing infrastructure code, understand the failure modes that bucket versioning prevents:

  1. Protection Against Human Error (Accidental Overwrites): If an engineer runs terraform apply with an incorrect variable set or forces an outdated state file, the valid remote state is overwritten. Versioning ensures the previous, healthy state file is preserved. S3 places the new state object on top of the old one, allowing rollbacks to the exact timestamp prior to the error.
  2. Protection Against Accidental Deletion: If a misconfigured CI/CD pipeline, rogue automation script, or operator deletes the state file, a versioned bucket does not permanently purge the underlying object. S3 simply places a Delete Marker on top of the object stack. Removing this Delete Marker restores the state file immediately.
  3. State Corruption & Network Failures: If a CI/CD runner crashes or drops its network connection while streaming an updated state file to AWS, versioning ensures the prior, uncorrupted state remains intact beneath the partial upload.
  4. Disaster Recovery & Ransomware Mitigation: If an unauthorized party compromises developer AWS credentials and attempts to purge state files, a versioned bucket combined with MFA Delete prevents permanent destruction of historical versions without access to a physical hardware or virtual MFA device.
  5. Auditing and Historical Forensics: When tracking down infrastructure drift, versioning allows you to download historical state files from weeks or months prior. Running a JSON diff between historical states pinpoints the exact time an attribute diverged.

docs.title: ⚠️ Directory Architecture: The Bootstrap Pattern
docs.text:
The S3 bucket, versioning configuration, and lifecycle policies provision the backend infrastructure that your application environments reference in their backend.tf blocks.

Because the backend bucket cannot exist inside the state file that it hosts, provision it in a standalone bootstrap/ directory using local state:

my-terraform-project/
├── bootstrap/             # Run ONCE locally to build the remote backend infrastructure
│   ├── versions.tf        # AWS Provider & CLI constraints (no backend block)
│   ├── providers.tf       # Provider definition & global tags
│   ├── main.tf            # State bucket, versioning, lifecycle rules, public access block
│   ├── outputs.tf         # Bucket name & ARN exports
│   └── terraform.tfstate  # Managed locally (Backed up securely outside Git)
└── environments/
    ├── dev/
    │   └── backend.tf     # References the bucket created by bootstrap/
    └── prod/
        └── backend.tf     # References the bucket created by bootstrap/

[!WARNING] 1. Run terraform apply inside bootstrap/ first before deploying any environment stacks. 2. Securely back up bootstrap/terraform.tfstate in an encrypted location (e.g., an encrypted vault or password manager). Losing this local state file impairs management of the backend bucket itself.

docs.title: bootstrap/versions.tf
docs.text:
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.10.0"

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }

  # Intentionally omitted: no backend block is declared here (Local State Bootstrap)
}

docs.title: bootstrap/providers.tf
docs.text:
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"

  default_tags {
    tags = {
      ManagedBy = "terraform-bootstrap"
      Project   = "my-company-prod"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: bootstrap/main.tf
docs.text:
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "terraform_state" {
  bucket = "my-company-prod-terraform-state"

  # Guardrail: Prevent accidental destruction via terraform destroy
  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}

[!NOTE] S3 bucket versioning can be set to Enabled or Suspended. Once enabled on a bucket, it cannot be fully disabled — suspending versioning only stops new versions from being generated; existing object versions remain intact.

docs.title: bootstrap/main.tf (Continued)
docs.text:
resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "terraform_state_versioning" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.terraform_state.id

  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

docs.title: Step 3: Lifecycle Rules (Cost & Storage Governance)
docs.text: State files update repeatedly across active CI/CD pipelines. Unmanaged version accumulation can quietly increase storage costs. Configure automated lifecycle expiration for non-current versions:

docs.title: bootstrap/main.tf (Continued)
docs.text:
resource "aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration" "state_lifecycle" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.terraform_state.id

  rule {
    id     = "expire-old-state-versions"
    status = "Enabled"

    noncurrent_version_expiration {
      noncurrent_days = 90 # Retain historical versions for 90 days, then purge
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Step 4: Configure Native S3 State Locking (Terraform $\ge$ 1.10)
docs.text: In Terraform 1.10+, the S3 backend supports native locking via S3 conditional writes, eliminating the requirement for a dedicated DynamoDB table:

docs.title: environments/dev/backend.tf
docs.text:
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "my-company-prod-terraform-state"
    key          = "dev/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "us-east-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true # Uses native S3 locking (.tflock file); replaces DynamoDB
  }
}

[!TIP] Legacy DynamoDB locking (dynamodb_table = "...") is maintained for backwards compatibility, but native S3 locking (use_lockfile = true) is the modern standard for new configurations.

docs.title: Phase 2: Testing & Verification
docs.text: Validate recovery procedures prior to an actual production incident.

docs.title: 1. Upload Initial State and Overwrite (Simulate Error)
docs.text:
# Upload Version 1 (Healthy)
echo '{"state": "v1-healthy"}' > terraform.tfstate
aws s3 cp terraform.tfstate s3://my-company-prod-terraform-state/terraform.tfstate

# Overwrite with Version 2 (Corrupted)
echo '{"state": "v2-corrupted"}' > terraform.tfstate
aws s3 cp terraform.tfstate s3://my-company-prod-terraform-state/terraform.tfstate

docs.title: 2. Verify Historical Object Versions
docs.text:
aws s3api list-object-versions \
  --bucket my-company-prod-terraform-state \
  --prefix terraform.tfstate

The output returns two records: * The newest version (IsLatest: true) corresponds to the corrupted V2. * The previous version corresponds to healthy V1, each identified by a unique VersionId.

docs.title: 🔥 Scenario A: State Was Overwritten or Corrupted
docs.text:
Objective: Roll back to the last known healthy state version.

  1. List object versions and locate the VersionId of the healthy state: 

    aws s3api list-object-versions \
  --bucket my-company-prod-terraform-state \
  --prefix terraform.tfstate

  2. Download the healthy version locally: 

    aws s3api get-object \
  --bucket my-company-prod-terraform-state \
  --key terraform.tfstate \
  --version-id "<HEALTHY_VERSION_ID>" \
  recovered_state.tfstate

  3. Inspect recovered_state.tfstate in an editor to confirm data integrity.

  4. Push the validated state file back to S3 as the new Latest version: 

    aws s3 cp recovered_state.tfstate s3://my-company-prod-terraform-state/terraform.tfstate

docs.title: 🔥 Scenario B: State File Was Accidentally Deleted
docs.text:
Objective: Remove the S3 Delete Marker to restore the object.

  1. List object versions and locate the active Delete Marker: 

    aws s3api list-object-versions \
  --bucket my-company-prod-terraform-state \
  --prefix terraform.tfstate

  2. Under the "DeleteMarkers" array in the output, find the entry where "IsLatest": true and copy its "VersionId".

  3. Delete the Delete Marker: 

    aws s3api delete-object \
  --bucket my-company-prod-terraform-state \
  --key terraform.tfstate \
  --version-id "<DELETE_MARKER_VERSION_ID>"

  4. Verify that the state file is restored: 

    aws s3 ls s3://my-company-prod-terraform-state/

docs.title: 🔥 Scenario C: State Lock Is Stuck
docs.text:
Objective: Clear a stuck state lock left behind by an interrupted apply or terminated CI/CD container.

If a process terminates unexpectedly mid-apply, Terraform may leave the state locked:

Error: Error acquiring the state lock
Lock Info:
  ID: 5f3c1a2e-8b4d-4a1f-9c3e-2d7a1b0f9c88
  Path: my-company-prod-terraform-state/prod/terraform.tfstate.tflock
  1. Confirm with your team and active CI/CD pipelines that no apply operation is currently executing.
  2. Force-release the stale lock using the lock ID: 
    terraform force-unlock 5f3c1a2e-8b4d-4a1f-9c3e-2d7a1b0f9c88

[!CAUTION] Never run force-unlock while an apply is active. Force-unlocking a live deployment can result in concurrent state writes and corruption.

docs.title: ✅ Part 4: Production Maintenance Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Versioning Enabled: Declared via aws_s3_bucket_versioning with status = "Enabled".
  • [ ] Non-Current Version Expiration: Configured in aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration (e.g., expire after 90 days).
  • [ ] Native S3 Locking: Configured with use_lockfile = true on Terraform $\ge$ 1.10.
  • [ ] Public Access Block: Configured via aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block to prevent public internet access.
  • [ ] Transport Security Policy: Attached an S3 bucket policy enforcing TLS (aws:SecureTransport = "true").
  • [ ] IAM Least Privilege: Restricted s3:DeleteObject* and s3:PutObject privileges to CI/CD service roles and platform leads.
  • [ ] MFA Delete: Enabled on the bucket for elevated protection against malicious version purging.
  • [ ] Encryption-at-Rest: Server-side encryption enabled (SSE-S3 or AWS KMS CMK) to protect secrets stored in the state file.
